Constitutional Arms Races in the Public Goods Game:
Co-Evolving LLM Constitutions Under Cooperation–Defection Pressure

Ujwal Kumar    Arth Singh    Hershraj Niranjani Affiliation: Shibaura Institute of Technology  NIT Agartala  UC Berkeley    Machiko Hirota    Takehiro Takayanagi Affiliation: University of Pennsylvania  The University of Tokyo    Alice Saito Affiliation: University of Pennsylvania  The University of Tokyo    Eiji Kamioka    Phan Xuan Tan ††thanks: Corresponding author: tanpx@shibaura-it.ac.jp
Abstract

Frontier LLM agents engage in blackmail, sabotage, and document leaks under goal conflicts in agentic settings, exposing limitations of alignment methods built around single-agent or cooperative assumptions. Recent work shows LLM-guided evolutionary search can discover effective cooperative constitutions, but two properties of the adversarial setting remain uncharacterized: whether the fitness function actually induces adversarial pressure, and whether the LLM mutation operator behaves reliably under adversarial-specialist objectives. We study adversarial constitutional co-evolution (Blue cooperators vs. Red free-riders, 30 generations) across a Public Goods Game (PGG) and a spatial grid-world. Three findings: (1) in the PGG, both factions converge to a near-parity equilibrium at S≈0.78S\approx 0.78, robust across tested multipliers m∈{1.2,1.5,2.0,3.0}m\in\{1.2,1.5,2.0,3.0\}; (2) in independently-scored environments, per-faction scoring leaves outcomes statistically uncoupled (corr​(SB,SR)=+0.088\text{corr}(S_{B},S_{R}){=}{+}0.088) and produces no adversarial pressure — a score-advantage fitness target Sown−SoppS_{\text{own}}{-}S_{\text{opp}} restores it; (3) under pure-adversary fitness, evaluation seed count KK controls mode-regression — K=2K{=}2 regresses, K=5K{=}5 sustains a strong specialist for all 30 generations. Adversarial co-evolution of natural-language constitutions is feasible, but only under coupled fitness and adequate evaluation budget; the evolved Red constitutions serve as interpretable red-team artifacts for testing future cooperative designs.

Keywords Multi-agent systems ⋅\cdot Constitutional AI ⋅\cdot Evolutionary Optimization ⋅\cdot LLM alignment ⋅\cdot Adversarial Co-evolution ⋅\cdot Public Goods Game

1 Introduction

Constitutional AI (CAI) aligns language models using human-written principles such as “be helpful and harmless” [1]. While effective for single-user interactions, this paradigm assumes that principles producing ethical behavior in isolation will scale to multi-agent settings. This assumption becomes increasingly fragile as LLM agents are deployed in settings where they negotiate, share information, compete for resources, use tools, and interact with other agents over extended horizons. In multi-agent environments, strategic incentives can amplify goal conflicts and lead to emergent coordination failures [2, 3]. Recent empirical work demonstrates that frontier LLM agents engage in deliberate harmful behaviors—including blackmail, sabotage, and confidential document leaks—when faced with goal conflicts in agentic settings [4]. These findings suggest that multi-agent alignment must be studied not only under cooperative assumptions, but also under adaptive adversarial pressure.

Background: cooperative constitutional evolution.

Kumar et al. [5] established that LLM-guided evolutionary search can discover effective cooperative constitutions in a multi-agent grid-world, substantially outperforming hand-crafted and one-shot LLM-designed baselines. In that setting, six homogeneous agents share a single constitution and collaborate on team projects. The evolved constitution C∗C^{*} consists of priority-ordered natural-language rules (e.g., “if carrying any resource your team needs, deposit immediately”) that agents follow verbatim at decision time. The key finding was that evolutionary search discovers operationally specific rules that outperform abstract principles. That work, however, evaluated only against static cooperative baselines in a single environment, leaving open questions about whether a cooperative constitution remains effective against an adaptive opponent, whether constitutional evolution behaves similarly across different social-dilemma structures, and whether an apparently adversarial objective actually creates adversarial selection pressure.

This work: adversarial constitutional co-evolution.

We introduce a framework in which two factions with opposing objectives alternately update their constitutions against the current opponent, creating a constitutional arms race. Each faction is governed by an interpretable, priority-ordered set of natural-language rules, and each generation updates one faction’s constitution against the current opponent. The framework serves three purposes: (i) it provides a robustness probe for cooperatively-evolved constitutions, (ii) it generates interpretable adversarial constitutions that can serve as red-team test cases for future research, and (iii) it lets us ask whether natural-language constitutional rules can track the game-theoretic equilibria of canonical social dilemmas.

We evaluate across two structurally different environments—a Public Goods Game (PGG) and a spatial grid-world. We organize the paper around the PGG result first, because the PGG’s shared-pool mechanics inherently provide the fitness coupling needed for adversarial dynamics. In contrast, the grid-world experiments initially use independently scored faction objectives; this difference lets us identify a methodological failure mode. Without coupled fitness, a run may appear adversarial while actually producing two independently productive factions rather than a genuine arms race.

Our contributions are:

  1. 1.

    PGG arms race. 30 generations of alternating co-evolution drive Blue cooperators from SB=0.370S_{B}{=}0.370 to 0.7770.777 and Red free-riders from SR=0.177S_{R}{=}0.177 to 0.7820.782, converging to a stable near-parity equilibrium robust across tested multipliers m∈{1.2,1.5,2.0,3.0}m\in\{1.2,1.5,2.0,3.0\} (Section 5.1).

  2. 2.

    Fitness coupling as a precondition for adversarial dynamics in independently-scored environments. Per-faction scoring inherited from [5] leaves outcomes statistically uncoupled when extended to two factions (corr​(SB,SR)=+0.088\text{corr}(S_{B},S_{R}){=}{+}0.088, SB+SRS_{B}{+}S_{R} varying). We propose score-advantage fitness Sown−SoppS_{\text{own}}{-}S_{\text{opp}} as the search target and show this single change enables measurable adversarial dynamics (Section 5.4).

  3. 3.

    Grid-world arms race under the corrected protocol. C∗C^{*} retains its lead under adversarial search (mean Red advantage −0.27-0.27); full co-evolution converges near parity; asymmetric information lets Red dominate (final Red advantage +0.415+0.415); a coordination requirement on attacks drops Red’s mean advantage to −0.66-0.66 without modifying the cooperator’s constitution (Sections 5.5–5.8).

  4. 4.

    Evaluation seed count KK controls mode-regression in LLM-guided pure-adversary search. At K=2K{=}2 search regresses; at K=5K{=}5 Red sustains a strong specialist for all 30 generations, isolating fitness-estimate noise as the readily-controllable lever (Section 5.9).

We do not claim that adversarially-evolved cooperative constitutions are more robust than cooperatively-evolved ones; testing that hypothesis would require a transfer experiment we have not run. Instead, this paper contributes a methodology for constructing and diagnosing constitutional arms races, showing when adversarial co-evolution works, when it silently fails, and what kinds of interpretable adversarial constitutions emerge under cooperation–defection pressure. This reframes constitutional alignment not only as a problem of designing good principles, but also as a problem of stress-testing governance rules against adaptive social conflict.

2 Background and Related Work

Constitutional AI and multi-agent alignment.

CAI aligns models using human-written principles and AI feedback [1, 6]. Extensions have improved helpfulness and reduced harmful outputs but maintain the single-agent paradigm. Carichon et al. [3] argue that alignment must become a “dynamic and social process” for multi-agent settings. Kumar et al. [5] operationalize this through evolutionary search over cooperative constitutions; we extend that line to adversarial co-evolution.

Multi-agent coordination and self-play.

Axelrod and Hamilton [7] showed that tit-for-tat evolves stable cooperation in iterated games; Leibo et al. [8] introduced sequential social dilemmas in multi-agent RL; Hughes et al. [9] and Jaques et al. [10] demonstrated that social preferences and influence rewards stabilize cooperation. Park et al. [11] showed emergent social behaviors in LLM agents. Competitive self-play trains strong policies in two-player games [12, 13]; however, self-play optimizes policy parameters rather than a natural-language governance artifact. Wang et al. [14] co-evolve agents and environments in single-agent curricula; we adapt this co-evolutionary structure to two-faction constitutional search. We do not update policy weights or generate code: we evolve interpretable priority-ordered natural-language rules that LLM agents follow verbatim at decision time.

Mechanism design and LLM-guided evolutionary search.

Our framework relates to automated mechanism design [15, 16, 17], where rules governing agent interaction are optimized for desired outcomes; we operate in partially observable environments where agent utility functions are implicit in LLM behavior rather than explicitly specified. The search machinery itself follows the FunSearch [18] and AlphaEvolve [19] line of LLM-as-mutation-operator program synthesis, with quality-diversity through ELM [20] and OpenEvolve [21] on MAP-Elites [22]. A common assumption in this line is that the LLM mutation operator faithfully implements the stated objective; our mode-regression result (Section 5.9) documents a case where this breaks under fitness-estimate noise.

Public goods games.

The PGG is a canonical model for cooperation and free-riding. Fehr and Gächter [23] showed that costly punishment sustains cooperation; Hauert et al. [24] showed that voluntary participation introduces cyclic dynamics; Rand et al. [25] showed that positive interactions promote cooperation. We use the PGG as a testbed for constitutional co-evolution that inherently provides the fitness coupling absent from independently-scored grid-world experiments.

3 Methodology

3.1 Constitutional Co-Evolution

We consider a multi-agent setting where nn agents are divided into two factions—Blue and Red. Each faction is governed by a constitution C={r1,…,rk}C=\{r_{1},\ldots,r_{k}\}, a priority-ordered set of natural-language rules that its agents follow at decision time. Faction observability is environment-dependent: in the grid-world, faction identities are hidden from agents, while in the PGG, faction roles are induced by the initialized cooperative or free-riding constitutions. Adversarial co-evolution produces a sequence of constitution pairs (CBg,CRg)(C^{g}_{B},C^{g}_{R}) for g=1,…,Gg=1,\ldots,G, where in each generation each faction’s constitution is updated to maximize its expected score against the most recent opponent constitution. We approximate each maximization with one iteration of LLM-guided evolutionary search via OpenEvolve [21] on top of MAP-Elites [22], alternating between Blue and Red. Three fitness targets appear in our experiments: absolute (SfactionS_{\text{faction}}), advantage (Sfaction−SoppS_{\text{faction}}{-}S_{\text{opp}}), and pure-adversary (1−Sopp1{-}S_{\text{opp}}, Red only). The reported stability score SS is identical in all modes; only the optimization target changes. The full algorithm and formal optimization definition are given in Appendix A.

3.2 Faction-Specific Scoring

We adapt the cooperative scoring of Kumar et al. [5] to the two-faction setting. Each faction is scored independently:

Sfaction=α⋅P+β⋅V−γ⋅CffS_{\text{faction}}=\alpha\cdot P+\beta\cdot V-\gamma\cdot C_{\text{ff}} (1)

where P∈[0,1]P\in[0,1] is productivity (faction-specific project progress in grid-world, pool utilization in PGG), V∈[0,1]V\in[0,1] is survival rate, and Cff∈[0,1]C_{\text{ff}}\in[0,1] is the friendly-fire rate. We use α=0.5\alpha{=}0.5, β=0.3\beta{=}0.3, γ=0.2\gamma{=}0.2 throughout.

Two changes from the cooperative scoring of Kumar et al. [5] are worth flagging: (i) the conflict term CC in the prior work counted all aggressive actions; in the adversarial setting we restrict it to within-faction aggression (CffC_{\text{ff}}), since cross-faction attacks are a legitimate strategic tool; (ii) the prior work clipped SS at zero; we allow S<0S<0 so that the search gradient is preserved when a faction is being dominated. Absolute SS values in this paper are therefore not directly comparable to those in [5]; only relative trends and inter-faction gaps are.

4 Environments

4.1 Grid-World with Hidden Adversarial Identity

We adapt the grid-world primitives of Kumar et al. [5] to a two-faction adversarial setting. The cooperative environment in that work divided six agents into two cooperating teams sharing a single constitution and a joint success criterion. We retain the resource types, action primitives, and per-step dynamics, and modify the setup as follows: two adversarial factions (Blue, Red) replace the cooperating teams, each with its own constitution; faction labels are hidden from agents; Blue and Red have symmetric project pairs (Shelter ++ Market vs. Fortress ++ Armory, identical resource requirements: 150 wood, 120 stone, 30 gems each); the grid is scaled from 6×66{\times}6 to 8×88{\times}8 to give two factions of three agents each room to operate; episodes are 40 turns; the action set (gather, deposit, move, communicate, attack at p=0.25p{=}0.25, steal at p=0.40p{=}0.40, give, rest) is inherited from the prior work; and the periodic Overseer-elimination and hunger mechanics are disabled, since they confound adversarial scoring (Appendix B details the rationale). We do not claim absolute comparability of SS values to [5]; the grid-world here is a related but distinct testbed.

4.2 Public Goods Game

To evaluate the method in a non-spatial social dilemma, we introduce a structurally different environment based on the classic PGG [23]. Six agents (3 Blue cooperators, 3 Red free-riders) play 20 rounds with multiplier m=1.5m{=}1.5 and initial endowment 100 per agent. Each round, agents choose to contribute (0–100% of wallet), punish (cost ratio 0.30.3 to punisher, 1.01.0 impact on target), broadcast a message, or rest. Scoring uses the same Eq. (1) formula with P=P= pool utilization, V=1.0V=1.0 (no death in PGG), and Cff=C_{\text{ff}}= within-faction free-riding rate.

The PGG captures a fundamentally different social dilemma: no spatial structure, no combat, no resource gathering. The shared pool inherently couples both factions’ payoffs — contributions feed the same pot, which is multiplied by mm and split equally — creating zero-sum strategic pressure without requiring any modification of the per-faction scoring.

5 Experiments

Organization. We present the main PGG result first (Section 5.1), then the PGG ablations (Sections 5.2, 5.3). We then turn to the grid-world. Adversarial dynamics in the grid-world require a fitness-coupling correction (Section 5.4), which we develop empirically before reporting Experiments 1–3 (Sections 5.5–5.8) and a defensive variant (Section 5.6). A final ablation on evaluation seed count (Section 5.9) isolates fitness-noise as the main driver of mode-regression in pure-adversary search.

5.1 PGG Co-Evolution

We run 30 generations of alternating co-evolution on the standard PGG (N=6N{=}6, m=1.5m{=}1.5, 20 rounds, endowment 100, K=2K{=}2 seeds) with Blue initialized from a cooperator seed (generous contribution, punish free-riders) and Red from a free-rider seed (minimal contribution, deceptive signaling). Seed constitutions are in Appendix F.

Both factions improve substantially. Blue climbs from SB=0.370S_{B}{=}0.370 to SB=0.777S_{B}{=}0.777 (+110%+110\%) and Red from SR=0.177S_{R}{=}0.177 to SR=0.782S_{R}{=}0.782 (+341%+341\%). Red catches up to Blue by generation 18, and both converge at a stable near-parity equilibrium around S≈0.78S\approx 0.78 for the final ten generations (Table 1, Figure 1).

The PGG pool is inherently shared: all agents’ contributions feed the same pot, which is multiplied by mm and split equally. This structural coupling creates adversarial selection pressure without requiring any modification of the per-faction fitness function — Red must discover that some level of contribution is necessary to avoid Blue’s punishment, and Blue must discover that punishment is necessary to sustain high contribution. The convergence at S≈0.78S\approx 0.78 is consistent with the high-cooperation rates reported by Fehr and Gächter [23] for PGGs with costly punishment, though we note that SS aggregates productivity, survival, and friendly-fire into a single scalar and is not a direct measure of contribution rate. The headline trajectory is a single K=2K{=}2 run; the multiplier ablation (Section 5.3) provides evidence that the equilibrium target is structural rather than seed-specific.

5.2 PGG under Pure-Adversary Fitness

A natural question is whether the convergence above depends on Red having its own productivity to optimize. We rerun the PGG with Red’s fitness target set to 1−SB1{-}S_{B} (pure-adversary, no productivity reward) starting from a pure-adversary seed. Across the 21 valid generations of a 30-generation run (gens 2–10 returned SB=SR=0S_{B}{=}S_{R}{=}0 from a recoverable LLM-mutation syntax-error pathology, Appendix E), Red maintains tight Blue suppression: SBS_{B} stays in [0.174,0.286][0.174,0.286] with mean 0.1980.198, and Red fitness averages 0.8020.802, with final fitness (0.7980.798) essentially equal to gen-1 fitness (0.8220.822). This contrasts with the grid-world (Section 5.9), where the same fitness mode at K=2K{=}2 exhibits mode-regression. We attribute the difference to PGG’s small action space (contribute, punish, broadcast, rest) compared to grid-world’s wider behavioral surface; with fewer non-adversarial actions available, the mutation operator’s productive-action prior has less material to drift toward. Environment structure, not just fitness signal, shapes whether adversarial search remains stable. The full per-generation trajectory is in Appendix C.

5.3 Multiplier Ablation: m∈{1.2,1.5,2.0,3.0}m\in\{1.2,1.5,2.0,3.0\}

To test whether the near-parity equilibrium is specific to m=1.5m{=}1.5, we rerun the same setup at m∈{1.2,2.0,3.0}m\in\{1.2,2.0,3.0\}, spanning the social-dilemma range (N=6N{=}6, so m=1.2m{=}1.2 sits near the lower bound and m=3.0m{=}3.0 near the upper). All four runs converge to near-parity with mean Red advantage in [−0.027,+0.005][-0.027,+0.005] over the final five generations (Table 2). The multiplier affects only the transient: at m=1.2m{=}1.2 both factions start low (SB=0.341S_{B}{=}0.341, SR=0.170S_{R}{=}0.170 at gen 1) and climb together; at m=3.0m{=}3.0 Red’s free-rider seed is heavily punished early (SR=0.287S_{R}{=}0.287 at gen 1) and catches up sharply by gen 5 (SR=0.727S_{R}{=}0.727). The steady state is the same high-cooperation equilibrium across all four conditions, indicating the result reflects the structural property of pool-based payoff coupling rather than a knife-edge multiplier calibration.

5.4 Fitness-Coupling Correction for Grid-World Experiments

The per-faction scoring in Eq. (1) references only within-faction quantities, so optimizing SRS_{R} independently yields no gradient toward strategies that degrade the opponent. We confirm this empirically: with Blue fixed at C∗C^{*} from [5] and Red evolving from a zero-sum seed under independent scoring, Pearson correlation between SBS_{B} and SRS_{R} across 30 generations is +0.088+0.088, and the sum SB+SRS_{B}{+}S_{R} varies over [1.09,1.31][1.09,1.31] — both inconsistent with a zero-sum game. Red’s SRS_{R} rises from 0.4830.483 to 0.6020.602 at generation 7 and plateaus in [0.49,0.60][0.49,0.60] thereafter, indicating Red has evolved productive self-building behavior rather than adversarial behavior (full diagnostic in Appendix E).

We therefore adopt a score-advantage fitness target for the grid-world experiments:

fitnessfaction=Sfaction−Sopponent.\text{fitness}_{\text{faction}}=S_{\text{faction}}-S_{\text{opponent}}. (2)

The reported stability score SS (Eq. (1)) is unchanged; only the search target changes. The formulation is symmetric, so the cooperative-vs-adversarial asymmetry is carried entirely by the initial seed constitutions.

5.5 Grid-World Experiment 1: C∗C^{*} Fragility under Adversarial Pressure

We fix Blue at C∗C^{*}, the best cooperative constitution from [5], and let Red evolve from a zero-sum seed for 30 generations under score-advantage fitness (8×88{\times}8 grid, 40 turns, K=2K{=}2 seeds, hidden faction identity).

C∗C^{*} exhibits structural resilience throughout. Red’s advantage SR−SBS_{R}-S_{B} remains negative for all 30 generations; the mean is −0.27-0.27 and the best (least negative) is −0.079-0.079 at generation 10 (per-generation values and trajectory plot in Appendix D). C∗C^{*}’s operational specificity (rules like “deposit immediately if carrying a needed resource”) confers adversarial robustness at this compute budget: Red closes the gap to within 0.080.08 but does not surpass it, and the trajectory shows no monotonic degradation. We do not claim that C∗C^{*} is robust in general — only that 30 generations of LLM-guided search at K=2K{=}2 does not break it. Stronger adversarial seeds, larger KK, or longer runs may yield different conclusions.

5.6 Defensive Variant: Coordination-Required Attacks

A natural defensive question: does the cooperative equilibrium become harder to break if attacks themselves require coordination? We rerun Exp 1 with attack success gated on faction adjacency: solo attacks succeed at p=0.05p{=}0.05 (vs. 0.250.25 baseline), coordinated attacks (one or more same-faction allies adjacent to the target) succeed at p=0.60p{=}0.60. The change is symmetric but matters only to Red, since C∗C^{*} does not attack. Across 30 generations, Red’s mean advantage drops to −0.663-0.663 (vs. −0.27-0.27 in the baseline Exp 1), and Red advantage is ≥0\geq 0 in only 1 of 30 generations. Red’s evolutionary search does discover that clustering attackers raises success, but coordinating multiple agents on the same target simultaneously across an 8×88{\times}8 grid with hidden faction identity is a coordination problem the LLM-mutation operator does not reliably solve. This points to a practical lever: spatial or temporal coordination requirements on damaging actions raise adversarial search difficulty without changing the fitness landscape or the cooperator’s rules. Full per-generation values in Appendix D.

5.7 Grid-World Experiment 2: Full Co-Evolution

We now let both factions evolve under symmetric score-advantage fitness: Blue from C∗C^{*} seed, Red from zero-sum seed, both optimizing Sown−SoppS_{\text{own}}-S_{\text{opp}} in alternating mode (30 generations, K=2K{=}2). The trajectory unfolds in three phases. In an early phase (gens 1–12), Blue holds a lead with Red advantage averaging −0.18-0.18; through gens 13–20 the gap closes; by gens 21–30 both factions oscillate near parity, with Red briefly establishing a lead at gens 26–27 before Blue partially recovers. Final values: SB=0.191S_{B}{=}0.191, Red advantage +0.192+0.192. The mean Red advantage across all 30 generations is −0.005-0.005, consistent with zero-sum search at near-parity. Score-advantage fitness produces a competitive equilibrium rather than the paralysis observed under independent scoring (where both factions collapsed toward zero within 15 generations in pilot runs). The absolute SS values are low because CffC_{\text{ff}} and the absence of the max⁡(0,⋅)\max(0,\cdot) floor allow negative scores; what matters here is the inter-faction gap, which oscillates around zero. Per-generation values and the four-panel trajectory plot in Appendix D.

5.8 Grid-World Experiment 3: Information Asymmetry Ablation

We rerun Exp 2 under two information conditions: (i) full—both factions observe all six agents’ action logs; (ii) asymmetric—Red observes all six agents, Blue observes only its own three. A third own-team condition (each faction sees only its own agents) hit the LLM-mutation syntax-error pathology before completion (Appendix E) and is not reported.

Information availability substantially shifts the equilibrium (Figure 2). Under full information, Blue holds an early lead (Red advantage averaging −0.18-0.18 through gen 24) before Red establishes a sustained lead in the final six generations (final Red advantage +0.267+0.267). Under asymmetric information, Red leads immediately (+0.264+0.264 at gen 1), reaches a maximum advantage of +0.503+0.503 at gen 20, drives Blue to SB=−0.367S_{B}{=}-0.367 at gen 17, and ends with Red advantage +0.415+0.415. With sustained intel disadvantage, Blue evolves rules that fail against the specific Red strategies it cannot fully observe. The final +0.415+0.415 in the asymmetric condition is the strongest Red result we observe in any grid-world experiment. Per-generation values for both conditions in Appendix D.

5.9 Evaluation Seed Count and Mode-Regression in Pure-Adversary Search

When Red has no productive goals of its own — fitness target 1−SB1-S_{B}, seed constitution restricted to adversarial rules — does evolutionary search converge on a stable specialist? With Blue fixed at C∗C^{*} and Red evolving from a 5-rule pure-adversary seed (hunt Blue, steal to disrupt, identify teammates, avoid friendly fire, no productive actions) for 30 generations, the answer at K=2K{=}2 is no. As reference, a hand-coded 20-line hunt-and-kill controller (move to nearest non-ally, attack when adjacent, no gathering) eliminates all Blue agents by turn 8 and yields SB=0.000S_{B}{=}0.000, fitness =1.0=1.0 — an upper bound on achievable pure-adversary performance.

At K=2K{=}2, Red’s fitness is non-monotonic: it peaks at generation 5 (SB=0.129S_{B}{=}0.129, fitness 0.8710.871), then degrades to fitness 0.5080.508 by generation 30 (SB=0.492S_{B}{=}0.492). From generation 15 onward, SRS_{R} drifts upward and rule count grows from 6 to 8–9 (Table 3), indicating re-acquisition of productive rules despite a seed that prohibits them and a fitness signal that does not reward them. Across all 30 generations, Red never approaches the adversarial capability of the hand-coded controller. This gap is real, and we do not paper over it: LLM-guided constitutional search underperforms a trivial specialist on raw adversarial capability. The value our framework adds lies elsewhere — the evolved Red constitutions are interpretable natural-language rules that can be inspected, transferred across seeds, and applied as red-team test cases against unseen cooperative constitutions, none of which the hand-coded controller offers.

Two ablations isolate the cause. (1) K=5K{=}5, 30 generations: increasing the evaluation seed count to K=5K{=}5 eliminates mode-regression entirely. Red sustains adversarial pressure throughout: SBS_{B} remains in [0.13,0.40][0.13,0.40] for all 30 generations, with peak SB=0.127S_{B}{=}0.127 at gen 18 and final fitness 0.8250.825 — substantially higher than the K=2K{=}2 endpoint (0.5080.508) and comparable to the K=2K{=}2 peak (0.8710.871). (2) G=60G{=}60, K=2K{=}2: extending the run to 60 generations shows that mode-regression is delayed but not eliminated at small KK. Red reaches a deeper minimum at gen 23 (SB=0.083S_{B}{=}0.083, fitness 0.9170.917) before drifting back; by gen 60, fitness returns to 0.5160.516.

The K=5K{=}5 result indicates that fitness-estimate noise is a measurable contributor to mode-regression: with five seeds the variance drops by ∼2.5×{\sim}2.5{\times}, and regression no longer occurs. The G=60G{=}60 result indicates that the mutation operator’s prior is also active — even at K=2K{=}2, the search reaches its deepest specialist at gen 23 rather than collapsing earlier. Mode-regression in LLM-guided evolution is best understood as the joint effect of fitness noise and operator prior. For adversarial-specialist search with LLM mutation, K≥5K\geq 5 should be considered a default rather than K=2K{=}2.

6 Cross-Environment Analysis

Across both environments under appropriately coupled fitness, we observe common properties. Both factions improve over generations and arms race dynamics emerge. Co-evolution discovers strategies that one-shot LLM design does not: communication minimization in the grid-world, punishment-calibrated contribution in the PGG. All evolved constitutions remain human-readable priority-ordered rules. Environment structure controls fitness-mode stability — pure-adversary fitness regresses in the grid-world but remains stable in the PGG, due to the narrower PGG action space. Mechanism design functions as a defensive lever: a single coordination requirement on attacks drops Red’s mean advantage from −0.27-0.27 to −0.66-0.66 without modifying any constitution. Final stability scores differ in absolute terms across environments (PGG: SB=0.777S_{B}{=}0.777, SR=0.782S_{R}{=}0.782; grid-world Exp 2: SB=0.191S_{B}{=}0.191, SR=0.192S_{R}{=}0.192; Exp 3-asymmetric: final Red advantage +0.415+0.415), but absolute SS comparisons across environments are not meaningful because SS aggregates different productivity components in each setting.

7 Discussion

Fitness coupling is a precondition for adversarial dynamics.

A central methodological contribution of this work is identifying that the natural per-faction scoring SfactionS_{\text{faction}} does not couple the two factions’ outcomes in independently-scored environments. Optimizing SRS_{R} independently produces a productive second faction rather than an adversary. The PGG’s shared-pool structure provides this coupling natively — and the clean arms race dynamics in Section 5.1, robust across m∈{1.2,1.5,2.0,3.0}m\in\{1.2,1.5,2.0,3.0\}, suggest that environments with explicit resource sharing may serve as more reliable testbeds for adversarial constitutional co-evolution than independently-scored games. For grid-world environments the coupling must be imposed explicitly via score-advantage fitness (Eq. (2)). This is an instance of a broader principle in mechanism design: the game’s payoff structure determines what evolutionary pressure actually selects for.

Evaluation seed count as a practical lever.

Section 5.9 surfaces evaluation seed count KK as a key hyperparameter for LLM-guided adversarial search: increasing KK from 2 to 5 eliminates mode-regression by reducing fitness-estimate noise. In contrast to prior work focused on mutation operator design [18, 19], this points to evaluation budget as an equally important axis.

Evolved Red constitutions as red-team artifacts.

The adversarial Red constitutions are themselves useful artifacts: each is a priority-ordered set of natural-language rules that produces measurable damage against a known cooperative constitution. The asymmetric-information Red (Exp 3, final advantage +0.415+0.415) and the K=5K{=}5 pure-adversary Red (Section 5.9, sustained SB∈[0.13,0.40]S_{B}\in[0.13,0.40]) are concrete red-team test cases that can be applied to evaluate future constitutional designs. Unlike adversarial neural policies, these artifacts are interpretable: practitioners can inspect the rules an attacker would follow and reason about which constitutional clauses they exploit.

What we do not claim.

We do not claim that adversarially-evolved cooperative constitutions are more robust than cooperatively-evolved ones. Testing that hypothesis would require running an adversarially-evolved Blue against a fresh adversarial Red and comparing against C∗C^{*} — an experiment we have not performed.

Limitations and broader impact.

Our framework relates to automated mechanism design [15, 16] where the “mechanism” is a natural-language constitution; the coordination-required attack result (Section 5.6) shows that mechanism and constitutional design are complementary. All headline trajectories are single K=2K{=}2 runs; variance across independent runs is not characterized. Two conditions hit a recoverable LLM-mutation syntax-error pathology and are reported with caveats; reruns are planned. The grid-world here differs from [5] in scoring and several mechanics (Appendix B), so absolute SS values are not directly comparable. Discovering governance rules through evolutionary optimization requires ongoing human oversight, and the adversarial Red constitutions are interpretable attack artifacts whose research value as red-team test cases must be weighed against misuse risk before any operational deployment.

8 Conclusion

Adversarial constitutional co-evolution works in environments with native fitness coupling: in the PGG, 30 generations drive both factions to a near-parity equilibrium at S≈0.78S\approx 0.78, robust across multipliers. In independently-scored environments the natural setup produces no adversarial pressure (corr​(SB,SR)=+0.088\text{corr}(S_{B},S_{R}){=}{+}0.088); a score-advantage fitness target restores it. The same operator regresses at K=2K{=}2 and stabilizes at K=5K{=}5, identifying evaluation noise as the primary controllable lever. The evolved Red constitutions are themselves interpretable red-team artifacts for future cooperative constitutions.

Appendix

Appendix A Formal Algorithm and Optimization Definition

The framework summary in Section 5.1 omitted formal details for brevity. Here we give them explicitly.

Definition A.1 (Co-Evolution).

Given environment ℰ\mathcal{E}, initial constitutions CB0,CR0C^{0}_{B},C^{0}_{R}, and scoring function SS, adversarial co-evolution produces a sequence of constitution pairs (CBg,CRg)(C^{g}_{B},C^{g}_{R}) for g=1,…,Gg=1,\ldots,G where each generation gg:

CBg\displaystyle C^{g}_{B} =arg​maxC⁡𝔼τ∼p⁡(τ|C,CRg−1,ℰ)​[SB​(τ)]\displaystyle=\argmax_{C}\;\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim p(\tau|C,C^{g-1}_{R},\mathcal{E})}[S_{B}(\tau)] (3)
CRg\displaystyle C^{g}_{R} =arg​maxC⁡𝔼τ∼p⁡(τ|CBg,C,ℰ)​[SR​(τ)]\displaystyle=\argmax_{C}\;\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim p(\tau|C^{g}_{B},C,\mathcal{E})}[S_{R}(\tau)] (4)

We approximate each maximization with one iteration of LLM-guided evolutionary search via OpenEvolve [21], alternating between Blue and Red. Algorithm 1 gives the procedure.

OpenEvolveStep runs one iteration of MAP-Elites evolutionary search [22] with an LLM mutation operator. The fitness target ϕ\phi determines the scalar OpenEvolve maximizes: ϕ=absolute\phi{=}\text{absolute} uses SfactionS_{\text{faction}}; ϕ=advantage\phi{=}\text{advantage} uses Sfaction−SoppS_{\text{faction}}{-}S_{\text{opp}}; ϕ=pure-adv\phi{=}\text{pure-adv} (Red only) uses 1−Sopp1{-}S_{\text{opp}}. The reported stability score SS is the same in all modes; only the search target changes.

Appendix B Grid-World Environment Changes from [5]

The grid-world environment in this paper inherits primitives from the cooperative grid-world of [5] but differs in several respects worth detailing for reproducibility.

Adversarial factions. The prior work divided six agents into two cooperating teams (Shelter, Market) sharing a single constitution. We replace this with two adversarial factions (Blue, Red), each with its own constitution and project pair. Symmetric resource requirements ensure neither faction has a structural advantage.

Hidden faction identity. Agents cannot see other agents’ faction labels. The prior work had no such restriction since all agents shared a team-cooperation goal.

Grid scale. We scale from 6×66{\times}6 to 8×88{\times}8 to give two factions of three agents each room to operate without forced contact on every turn. With 6×66{\times}6 and adversarial dynamics, encounters become trivially frequent and the strategic surface compresses.

Conflict scoring. The prior work’s CC counted all aggressive actions. In our adversarial setting cross-faction attacks are a legitimate strategic tool, so we restrict the conflict term to CffC_{\text{ff}} (within-faction aggression only). Same-faction friendly fire remains penalized.

max⁡(0,⋅)\max(0,\cdot) floor removed. The prior work clipped SS at zero. We allow S<0S<0 so that the search gradient is preserved when a faction is being dominated; this is why SBS_{B} goes negative in some experiments (e.g., SB=−0.367S_{B}{=}-0.367 at gen 17 of Exp 3-asymmetric).

Overseer disabled. The periodic-elimination mechanic confounds adversarial scoring — a Red “win” from killing Blue agents is indistinguishable from a Red “win” from Overseer elimination of Blue agents. We disable it.

Hunger disabled. The optional starvation mechanic is removed to isolate strategic dynamics from resource-based attrition.

Appendix E Diagnostic Run: Independent Scoring Does Not Produce Adversarial Dynamics

This appendix documents the diagnostic argument in Section 5.4: that independent per-faction scoring does not impose adversarial selection pressure on Red.

Setup.

Blue fixed at C∗C^{*} from [5], Red evolving from a zero-sum seed, 30 generations, K=2K{=}2 seeds, fitness target SRS_{R} (per-faction independent scoring).

Statistics.

Pearson correlation between SBS_{B} and SRS_{R} across 30 generations: +0.088+0.088. Sum SB+SRS_{B}{+}S_{R} varied over [1.09,1.31][1.09,1.31] with standard deviation 0.0550.055. Red’s SRS_{R} rose from a starting 0.4830.483 to a maximum of 0.6020.602 at generation 7 and plateaued in [0.49,0.60][0.49,0.60] thereafter. Blue’s SBS_{B} stayed in [0.65,0.73][0.65,0.73] for all 30 generations.

Inference.

A zero-sum game would imply negative correlation between the factions’ scores and approximately constant sum. Neither holds. Under independent scoring, Red’s evolutionary search has no gradient toward strategies that degrade Blue: SRS_{R} is a function only of Red-side quantities. Red therefore evolves productive self-building behavior — gathering resources for its own projects — rather than adversarial behavior. Replacing the search target with score-advantage SR−SBS_{R}{-}S_{B} (Section 5.4) couples the factions’ outcomes and produces the qualitatively different dynamics reported in Sections 5.5–5.8.

Note on the LLM-mutation syntax-error pathology.

Two conditions in this paper (the own-team variant of Exp 3, and gens 2–10 of the PGG pure-adversary run) returned SB=SR=0S_{B}{=}S_{R}{=}0 from a recoverable failure mode of the LLM mutation operator. The operator periodically produces Python with syntax errors; at K=2K{=}2 seeds, these broken constitutions occasionally win the OpenEvolve database round. The orchestrator we used at the time did not validate constitutions before saving them as the next-generation seed; once a broken constitution became the parent for further mutations, every child also failed to load and scored 0, poisoning the lineage. In the PGG pure-adversary run, the OpenEvolve database recovered from a valid earlier seed at generation 11. In the own-team Exp 3 condition, the run completed before recovery. We have since added syntax validation before checkpointing, but the affected runs are not recoverable without reruns, which are planned for the camera-ready version.

Appendix F Constitution Specifications

F.1 Grid-World: Initial Blue Constitution (C∗C^{*} Cooperative Seed, from [5])

  1. 1.

    Deposit First (Priority 1): If carrying any resource your team needs, deposit immediately.

  2. 2.

    Survival Focus (Priority 2): Keep deposit count above elimination threshold.

  3. 3.

    Gather & Deposit (Priority 3): Collect needed resources when empty.

  4. 4.

    Dynamic Targeting (Priority 4): Move toward largest team deficit.

  5. 5.

    Share Resources (Priority 5): Transfer surplus to nearby teammates.

  6. 6.

    Report Rich Cluster (Priority 6): Broadcast only for 2+ resources.

  7. 7.

    Conflict Avoidance (Priority 7): No aggression unless attacked.

F.2 Grid-World: Initial Red Constitution (Zero-Sum Seed)

  1. 1.

    Sabotage Opponents (Priority 1): Attack or steal from opposing team.

  2. 2.

    Hoard Resources (Priority 2): Gather but delay depositing.

  3. 3.

    Self-Preservation (Priority 3): Focus on personal survival.

F.3 PGG: Initial Blue Constitution (Cooperator Seed)

  1. 1.

    Contribute Generously (Priority 1): Contribute at least 60% each round.

  2. 2.

    Conditional Cooperation (Priority 2): Reduce if group average drops below 30%.

  3. 3.

    Punish Free-Riders (Priority 3): Punish agents contributing <<10% for 2+ rounds.

  4. 4.

    Communicate Norms (Priority 4): Broadcast cooperation expectations.

  5. 5.

    Maintain Fairness (Priority 5): Match or exceed group average.

F.4 PGG: Initial Red Constitution (Free-Rider Seed)

  1. 1.

    Minimise Contribution (Priority 1): Contribute at most 15%.

  2. 2.

    Exploit Cooperators (Priority 2): Contribute 0% when others contribute highly.

  3. 3.

    Avoid Detection (Priority 3): Occasionally contribute 20–30% to avoid punishment.

  4. 4.

    Deceptive Signalling (Priority 4): Announce high contributions, contribute low.

  5. 5.

    Late-Round Defection (Priority 5): Cooperate early, defect after round 3.
